newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil open to further car import quota talks.
newsitem.headline: Brazil open to further car import quota talks.

text.p: Brazil is open to new talks on import quotas granted certain major car manufacturing countries, and has little preference for whether the quotas should be disbanded or continued, a senior Brazilian diplomat said.

Jose Alfredo Graca Lima, head of the Foreign Ministry's Economics Department, said neither the European Union nor Japan, two principal beneficiaries of the quota system which expires on August 20, had yet approached Brasilia with formal proposals.

"When we established the quota we said then it would be for one year. But nothing prevents the scheme from being extended and, at the same time, nothing prevents it from being suspended," Graca Lima told reporters.

The low tariff quota system was awarded to Japan, the European Union and South Korea last year in compensation for a Car Industry Regime that sets lower import taxes for car makers with factories in Brazil.
Graca Lima was speaking shortly after two auto companies, seeking to take advantage of the regime, joined a long line of competitors in announcing new investment plans for Brazil.
Japan's Honda Motor Co Ltd will build a $300 million motorcycle plant in the state of Goias, Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles said.
And Czech truck builder Skoda intends to construct two $150 million factories, one in the southern state of Santa Catarina and the other in the northeast, in the state of Bahia.
The Car Industry Regime, which allows domestic producers to import at half the usual 63 percent tariff, has been the subject of formal WTO talks with the EU and the United States.
But it has also attracted at least $10 billion in investment by international car makers.
Under the quota scheme, Japan, the European Union and South Korea can import into Brazil at a special 35 percent tariff a total of 50,000 vehicles up to August 20.
Diplomats said the European Union wants the quota increased, principally because of pressure from carmaker Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG and its subsidiary Land Rover.
Both have announced plans to build factories in Brazil but would like to benefit from the quota system before they can start bringing in vehicles under the Car Industry Regime.
The Japanese feel less combative, diplomats said.
"We know Brazil faces problems with a widening trade and current account gap," a Japanese official said privately.
Graca Lima played down the significance of the quota system to Brazil's balance of payments situation.
He noted that Brazilian car exports were expected to total some $3.0 billion this year, largely due to new investment, and said the 50,000 vehicles in the quota added up to $500 million.
"The quota is a fraction of what is exported," he said.
He added that Brazil had to be attentive to its external accounts. "The situation must be monitored," he said.
Brazil is posting a a $4.0 billion trade gap so far this year compared with a $5.5 billion deficit for the whole of 1996.
Its current account gap in the balance of payments is running at about 3.9 percent of gross domestic product against 3.25 percent for last year.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358))
